title: How to work a three-quarter cross-stitch
subtitle: The fractional stitch for softened edges and diagonal curves
excerpt: A three-quarter cross-stitch is the most common fractional stitch in counted cross-stitch. It fills three corners of an Aida square and shares the fourth with a quarter stitch from an adjacent square, which is how curved outlines in a chart become smooth rather than stepped.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, fractional stitch chapter. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch that covers three corners of an Aida square: the full first diagonal of a cross-stitch, plus a half-diagonal running from the opposite corner to the centre hole. Paired with a quarter stitch from an adjacent square to fill the shared square.
A half-diagonal stitch running from one corner of the Aida square to the centre hole. Pairs with a three-quarter cross-stitch from an adjacent corner to fill the same square.
The hole at the intersection of four Aida squares, reached by pushing the needle through the weave of the fabric rather than through a standard grid hole. The destination for all fractional stitches.

content.text: is a full diagonal plus one half-diagonal that ends at the centre of the square. It covers three corners of an
square instead of the usual four. Charts use it at the edges of shapes to suggest a curve or diagonal rather than a stepped block outline.
The square is shared with a
from the neighbouring colour, both meeting at the
. On 14-count Aida, use two strands for both stitches. On evenweave worked over two threads, the centre hole is found at the intersection of the threads rather than through the weave.

Bring the needle up at corner 1 (bottom-left of the square on 14-count Aida). Push it down at corner 4 (top-right). This is the first diagonal of the full cross and the long arm of the three-quarter stitch.

Bring the needle back up at corner 3 (bottom-right). Now pierce the centre of the square, pushing the needle through the weave to the centre hole. The half-diagonal should lie over the first diagonal, crossing it at the centre.

On 14-count Aida, push the needle firmly through the centre of the woven block. The point passes between threads rather than through a grid hole. Feel for the gap and push steadily; the needle should slip through without forcing.

Check the stitch from the front. The half-diagonal should sit smooth against the long arm, both legs of the stitch ending at the same centre point. If the half-diagonal has missed the centre, unpick and try again.
Work the adjacent quarter stitch in the neighbouring colour. It rises from the fourth corner of the shared square and drops to the same centre hole from the opposite angle.

items.symptom: The needle won't go through the centre of the Aida
items.cause: Aida is woven with closely-set threads; the centre point is the gap between four threads, not a clear hole like a grid hole.
items.fix: Hold the fabric up to the light to see the centre intersection, then press the needle tip into the gap firmly. A size 22 needle passes through more easily than a size 24 on 14-count; use the larger size if you're struggling.

items.symptom: The half-diagonal doesn't reach the centre neatly
items.cause: The needle came up too far from the corner, or the half-diagonal was pulled at an angle.
items.fix: The stitch must start exactly at the grid-hole corner (not part-way along the fabric thread) and travel in a straight line to the centre. Unpick and re-position the starting point.

content.text: Once the three-quarter and quarter stitches work cleanly together, try a small chart that uses them to suggest animal fur or flower petals. The difference between a stepped outline and a smooth edge is visible even on a 30-stitch design.
